cues.text:
For a while, the front doors
of Galveston opened onto empty air.

Beneath the houses stood
forests of wooden supports.

Above the muddy ground,
narrow walkways led people home.
This was not the storm itself.
This was the rebuilding.

And it began
with an extraordinary question:

how do you save a city when
the ground beneath it is too low?
At the turn of the twentieth century,

Galveston was one of the busiest
ports in the American South.
Cotton moved through its docks.
Trains brought goods and visitors.
Ships connected Texas to the wider world.

But Galveston had a weakness that
could not be seen on a ledger.

The city stood on a long,
low barrier island off the Texas coast.
The highest natural ground on the island

was estimated to be
less than nine feet above sea level.

The sea was part of its prosperity, but it
was also close enough to become a threat.

In June 1900, the census counted almost
thirty-eight thousand people in the city.
Families lived in wooden houses.
Children walked to school.
Shopkeepers opened their doors.

For most of them, September 8 began
like another day on the Gulf Coast.

Days earlier, a tropical
storm had crossed Cuba.

It strengthened as it
moved across the Gulf.

At the time, there were
no weather satellites,
no radar maps on a phone,

and no way for forecasters
to follow a hurricane

over open water with anything
like modern precision.

Reports came from scattered observations,
ships, and telegraph stations.

A storm warning flag was raised
in Galveston on September 7.
The danger was not entirely unknown.

But many residents did not expect
the catastrophe that was approaching.
Some had experienced earlier storms

and believed their city
could withstand another.

Isaac Cline, the local Weather Bureau
official, watched conditions change.

The next day the sea was rising,
the wind was strengthening,
and the information reaching the public

could not show the full
scale of what was coming.

On the morning of September 8,
water began creeping into the streets.
Then the Gulf pushed farther inland.

By afternoon, people who
had expected bad weather
were confronting something far worse.

The water was not simply rain
collecting in low places.

The hurricane drove a massive
surge across the island.

The storm surge was later
estimated at nearly sixteen feet.

Waves carried timbers, pieces of houses,
and everything else they could tear loose.

As debris struck buildings,
some walls gave way.

Other structures were lifted
from their foundations.

People climbed to upper floors
and gathered in stronger buildings.
Families took in neighbors.

One building that survived was
the Gresham family's stone house,
known today as Bishop's Palace.
According to accounts of survivors,

more than two hundred
residents found refuge there.

Yet height offered little certainty as
water and wreckage moved through the city.
At the Weather Bureau,
the wind gauge recorded gusts of roughly

one hundred miles an hour
before it blew away.

Conditions grew more violent
into the evening.
Darkness made it harder to see

where the water ended or what
was coming toward a house.
Cline and his family struggled to survive.
His wife died in the storm.

Their loss was one among
thousands across Galveston,

and many families would
never be whole again.

Near midnight, the wind and water
finally began to subside.

What daylight revealed
was a city transformed.
Streets were buried beneath wreckage.
Houses had disappeared or been torn apart.

Survivors searched for relatives among
unfamiliar piles of broken timber.

The death toll could never be
counted with complete certainty.
At least six thousand people died.
Some estimates are considerably higher,
and the storm remains the deadliest

weather-related natural disaster
in United States history.

The city faced an immediate task
as terrible as the storm itself:

caring for the living
and finding the dead.
Temporary morgues were established.
As the scale of the losses became clear,

recovery workers struggled with more
bodies than the city could handle.

Aid came from outside,
but the future was uncertain.

Galveston could rebuild
its homes and businesses.

Yet if another hurricane
drove water over the island,

the same low ground would
be waiting beneath them.

Rebuilding also meant
living with uncertainty.

A replacement house could be
swept away by a future surge.

Businesses needed a functioning
port, families needed homes,

and the island needed a way to face
the water that surrounded it.

The question was no longer
simply how to restore the city.

It was how to give it
a better chance next time.

A board of engineers proposed
two connected defenses.
First came a seawall along the Gulf side:

a massive barrier designed to meet
the waves before they reached the streets.

But a wall alone would
leave a problem behind it.

Much of the city still
lay close to sea level.

The second part of the plan
was almost harder to imagine.
They would raise the ground.
And before the ground could rise,

buildings standing on it
would have to rise too.

Work on the first section
of the seawall began in 1902.

a concrete barrier
about three point three miles
long stood along the Gulf.

Its top rose seventeen feet
above mean low water.

Later extensions would carry
the wall farther along the coast.
While the seawall was being built,

the grade-raising project
turned neighborhoods
into construction sites behind it.
The work moved from section to section.

Crews lifted buildings on
hand-operated screw jacks
and supported them on temporary timbers.
About two thousand buildings were raised,

according to the
American Society of Civil Engineers.
That number tells only part of the story.

A building could not simply be set aside
while a new foundation was prepared.

It had to remain supported as crews
worked below and around it.
And every raised house stood among streets

and services that needed
to connect at a new level.

Water pipes, fire hydrants,
and streetcar tracks

also had to be dealt with as the level
of the ground changed.

This was not a model
on an engineer's desk.
It was a living city,

full of structures that
had to be kept in place
while the land around them was remade.

To bring in the material, a canal
was cut through part of Galveston.

Dredges collected sand
and carried it through the canal.

Workers then pumped fill
into the areas being raised,

including spaces beneath
the lifted buildings.
The amount varied from place to place.

The aim was not to lift every
street to exactly the same height,

but to create a higher,
sloping grade behind the seawall.
What looked like chaos had a purpose:

sand gradually became the new ground
on which the city would stand.
Once an area was filled to its new grade,

foundations could be finished
beneath the structures.

Work could then move
on to another section.

The change was gradual, not a single
dramatic lift of the entire island.

Some residents continued living
in their houses during the work.

To get around, they used makeshift
boardwalks raised above the muddy fill.
Imagine stepping out of a front door

onto a narrow wooden path while
crews reshaped the ground below.
The transformation also came at a cost.
Taxpayers helped finance the work,

and property owners had to pay
for lifting their buildings.

As streets and sidewalks
disappeared beneath fill,

residents faced the expense
of replacing them too.
The engineering solution was remarkable,

but rebuilding placed real burdens
on the people who remained.

One of the most striking challenges
was Saint Patrick's Church.

The building weighed
an estimated three thousand tons.

According to the
Galveston and Texas History Center,

workers used seven hundred jacks
to raise it five feet.
A heavy masonry church,

moved upward not by
a single enormous machine,

but by the patient coordination
of many smaller lifts.
The main work continued for years.

Temporary supports disappeared
beneath new foundations.

The temporary canal was filled
back in. Streets were rebuilt.
Little by little,

the strange city of boardwalks and raised
houses gave way to a more familiar one.

Then another hurricane put
the defenses to the test.

In 1915, a powerful
storm struck the region.
Galveston suffered damage,

but the loss of life in the city
was far lower than in 1900.
The seawall and raised ground had become

part of a broader response to a danger
the city now understood much better.
That did not make Galveston invulnerable.

Hurricanes continued
to threaten the island,

and in 2008 Hurricane Ike brought
a major surge to the Texas coast.
No wall can erase the sea

or guarantee that every future
storm will be survived without loss.

But the people of Galveston had
done something extraordinary.

After a disaster that
destroyed thousands of lives,
they chose not only to rebuild their city.
They changed the ground beneath it.
For years, homes stood above muddy streets

while workers brought in the sand that
would make a different future possible.

The storm had revealed how
vulnerable Galveston was.

The answer was written, piece by piece,
into the shape of the city itself.
